title: Bay of Bengal cyclone could bring rain, snow to Nepal next week - The Kathmandu Post
description: Bay of Bengal cyclone could bring rain, snow to Nepal next week  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Clear skies following the end of Nepal’s monsoon could give way to unsettled weather next week as a low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal is forecast to intensify into a cyclonic storm, potentially bringing rain to parts of Nepal and snowfall in the high Himalayas.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, in a special post-monsoon weather bulletin issued on Friday, warned that the system could affect Nepal from October 28 to November 1. Meteorologists have urged farmers to protect their ripening paddy crops and trekkers to exercise caution in high-altitude areas.

According to the department, a low-pressure area formed over the east-central and adjoining southeastern Bay of Bengal at 5:45 am on Friday. The system is expected to strengthen, move west-northwestwards and develop into a cyclonic storm by Monday before moving towards the coast of northern Andhra Pradesh and adjoining southern Odisha in India.

The department said it was too early to determine the amount of rainfall Nepal could receive or the level of risk, but warned that the weather system could affect agriculture and tourism.

The India Meteorological Department said in a bulletin issued on Saturday that the system was strengthening. It forecast that the low-pressure area would intensify into a depression and then a deep depression on Sunday before developing into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday morning.

The system is expected to strengthen further as it moves west-northwestwards, reaching the west-central Bay of Bengal near the Andhra Pradesh coast by Wednesday morning.

Meteorologist Binod Pokharel, who shared a weather analysis on social media, warned of potential weather-related risks across Nepal from October 29 to November 1. Current forecasts indicate rain across much of the country, with heavy downpours possible in some areas.

He said the risk of rainfall would be relatively high on October 30 and 31. The forecast points to possible weather-related risks in Kathmandu and 28 districts across Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces. Manang also warrants particular attention, he said.

Pokharel noted that the low-pressure system from the Bay of Bengal could interact with an upper-level trough, increasing the likelihood of heavy rainfall.

He urged farmers to monitor local forecasts and make arrangements to protect ripening paddy still standing in fields, as well as harvested crops laid out to dry, from potential damage.

Climate and environment expert Ujjwal Upadhyay also forecast rainfall across the country from October 28 to November 1. He urged farmers to harvest and bring in their crops and recommended suspending trekking in the high Himalayas during the period.

Upadhyay said the weather system could affect Nepal for nearly a week, although that did not necessarily mean continuous rainfall. There could be breaks in the rain, but the weather was unlikely to clear completely, with further showers possible at intervals, he said.

As the system continues to develop, rainfall could intensify, with hail also possible in some places, Upadhyay warned.

title: Former President urges global community to seriously take climate justice - The Rising Nepal
description: Former President urges global community to seriously take climate justice  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 24: Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari said the unprecedented natural disasters Nepal has experienced this year have once again underscored the gravity of this challenge, prompting a call to the global community to take Nepal's demand for climate justice seriously.

Addressing the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) conference organized by the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs, today, she outlined the state of climate justice that Nepal needs to achieve, according to her secretariat.

Bhandari cited examples linking global governance with climate justice while noting the Himalayas are a shared natural heritage closely connected to regional water cycles, biodiversity and ecological balance.

'In order to protect this vital ecosystem and mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change, it is essential to strengthen cooperation among Himalayan countries, including China, Nepal and India, in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers, developing early warning systems and coordinating disaster response,' she argued.

She also emphasized ensuring regional and international cooperation to strengthen to reduce climate risks, while ensuring sustained and reliable support from the United Nations and international financial institutions.

'Nepal advocates a world order in which relations among nations are guided not by power, but by international law, in which the voices of all nations are respected; and in which the concerns of weaker and vulnerable countries receive due consideration.' she asserted.

The former President emphasized the need to strengthen the United Nations as an effective institution that reflects the diversity and aspirations of the contemporary world to that end.

Peace and development are mutually reinforcing, she said, adding that ending poverty and hunger, promoting human well-being and redirecting resources spent on the arms race towards development are shared responsibilities of the international community.

'In accordance with the principle of leaving no one behind, we must make cooperation more effective in advancing inclusive, resilient and environmentally sustainable development.' Bhandari added.

She expressed her confidence that this forum will foster meaningful deliberations towards making the global governance system more just, inclusive and effective, while creating new opportunities for cooperation in pursuit of world peace, sustainable development and shared prosperity.

Highlighting that Nepal–China relations have evolved since ancient times through cultural exchanges, Buddhist philosophy and close people-to-people ties, Bhandari elucidated that our relationship rests on mutual respect, trust and cooperation. Also on the occasion, she expressed Nepal’s unequivocal commitment to the One-China Policy.

Respect for sovereign equality and for one another’s independence and territorial integrity is fundamental to sustaining enduring friendship and trust among nations, she stressed, calling for dialogue, cooperation and collective commitment to address the global challenges.

'The international order founded on the Charter of the United Nations, international law and multilateralism has made significant contributions to international peace, security and development. Nevertheless, reforms are necessary to make this system more inclusive, representative, transparent and effective in keeping with the changing global context,' the former President noted.(RSS)

title: Continuous surveillance needed to maintain polio-free status - The Rising Nepal
description: Continuous surveillance needed to maintain polio-free status  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 24: Chairperson of the World Health Organization’s South-East Asia Regional Certification Commission for Polio Eradication, Prof Dr Srijana Shrestha, has highlighted the vital need for continuous surveillance and sustained efforts to maintain Nepal’s polio-free status.

In a video message released today on the occasion of World Polio Day, she noted that while Nepal’s achievements in polio eradication are remarkable, sustained efforts are required to ensure this status is maintained indefinitely.

Pointing out that as long as the poliovirus persists anywhere in the world, there remains a risk of the disease entering Nepal, she emphasized the need for constant vigilance, especially given the country’s open borders and cross-border mobility of people.

She outlined the importance of ensuring that routine immunization services reach every child particularly those in remote or high-risk areas and communities to guarantee they receive full vaccination. Furthermore, "acute flaccid paralysis" (AFP) surveillance for the timely detection of the poliovirus needs to be prioritized along with regular reviews of surveillance data to ensure a rapid and effective response, should the virus be detected.

Given the shifting landscape of global financial support for polio, it is crucial to preserve essential capacities and infrastructure such as surveillance systems, laboratory services, immunization programs, and outbreak response mechanisms for all vaccine-preventable diseases.

Dr Shrestha also emphasized the need to leverage the experience, expertise, and infrastructure gained through polio eradication efforts to strengthen the surveillance and response systems for other vaccine-preventable diseases.(RSS)

title: $1.3 Billion Indo-US Satellite Saw Nepal Disaster Coming. But No One Saw It - NDTV
description: $1.3 Billion Indo-US Satellite Saw Nepal Disaster Coming. But No One Saw It  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
The world's single most expensive civilian Indo-US Earth imaging satellite, NISAR, costing $1.3 billion, saw the warning signs in the Nepal Himalayas. But nobody was watching, and hence no warning was issued.

Experts say merely putting what can only be called 'White Elephants' in the sky is not good enough; one needs human intelligence combined with artificial intelligence to accurately issue early warnings. After all, over a billion human lives are at risk in the northern Indian plains, and NISAR still has four years of life left to redeem itself.

The real mystery is why nobody was watching the data as it was beamed down every 12 days. The evidence was embedded in the voluminous data, but neither ISRO nor NASA connected the dots. Here is a plaintive chronicling of the lessons from NISAR's unheard alert.

Also Read: Nepal Flood: Was World's Most Expensive Eye In The Sky NISAR Caught Napping?

The devastating Nepal Rasuwa flash flood of August 26 is emerging as a defining lesson for scientists, disaster managers and governments across the Himalayan region. The world's single most expensive civilian Earth observation satellite, the $1.3 billion NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission, had in fact detected subtle movements in the glacier and rock mass that ultimately collapsed as it was supposed to do. But the signals were only discovered after the disaster, underscoring a hard truth of modern Earth observation: detecting danger is one thing; continuously monitoring and interpreting enormous volumes of satellite data in real time and issuing a timely warning is quite another.

Hence, some are dubbing the 2393 kg NISAR satellite launched on July 30, 2025, from Sriharikota a white elephant in the sky.

The findings come from the first scientific paper published on the Nepal disaster by 12 scientists from ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad. The study reconstructs the entire chain of events that led to one of the deadliest Himalayan disasters in recent memory and reveals that NISAR had detected "precursory movement" in the mountains weeks before the catastrophic collapse. But no one took heed.

On the morning of August 26, a massive section of glacier ice and permafrost rock detached from a hanging glacier north of Langtang Lirung peak in Nepal at an altitude of about 5,130 metres. The collapse triggered a gigantic rock-ice avalanche that rapidly transformed into a flood and debris flow racing through the Lhende Khola and Trishuli river systems. The resulting devastation spread across a 72-kilometre stretch of river valley, destroying roads, bridges, buildings, tunnels and critical infrastructure in Nepal and along the Nepal-China border trade corridor.

According to figures cited in the latest ISRO study from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the disaster had claimed 1,451 lives, while 5,745 people remained missing as of September 21, 2026. Additional fatalities were also reported in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.

Satellite analysis showed that the initial collapse involved an astonishing 99 million cubic metres of rock and ice. To put that in perspective, the volume was equivalent to about 115 Empire State Buildings crashing down a Himalayan mountainside almost simultaneously.

What made the event so destructive was not merely the size of the collapse but the enormous release of energy. The detached mass plunged about 1,300 metres from the source region to the glacier valley floor before continuing downslope through an additional vertical drop of nearly 870 metres. In total, the debris mass descended roughly 2,170 metres. That immense loss of elevation converted gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, accelerating and pulverising the rock and ice into a highly mobile mixture of debris, water and meltwater capable of tearing through a narrow valley in minutes.

The paper published in the Journal of Indian Society of Remote Sensing describes how the avalanche travelled nearly 5.9 kilometres along the valley floor, entraining additional snow, glacier ice, rocks and sediments before transforming into a devastating flash flood. Scientists also recorded a secondary landslide about three hours later, which further complicated the disaster by creating a debris-dammed lake.

The latest paper also states that the earthquake signature detected at 8.22 AM Indian time was an acoustic signal of the rock avalanche coming down with a huge impact, and the earthquake did not trigger the rock-ice avalanche.

The most significant scientific revelation, however, comes from NISAR.

The satellite was launched with considerable expectations because of its ability to measure movement of the Earth's surface with extraordinary precision. It has often been described as capable of detecting ground motion down to millimetre scales. Monitoring glaciers, glacier dynamics, land deformation and natural hazards across mountain regions such as the Himalayas is one of its important objectives.

The NRSC study found that NISAR's L-band radar data covering the period from June 20 to August 19, 2026 clearly identified an unstable high-velocity zone exactly where the catastrophic collapse later occurred. The results showed accelerating deformation and creep in the escarpment section before failure. In the final monitoring interval between July 26 and August 19, displacement vectors became larger, more coherent, and spread across much of the eventual collapse zone. Some pixels recorded cumulative horizontal offsets exceeding five metres.

The data effectively captured the mountain moving before it broke apart. But the warning remained buried within the vast ocean of satellite observations.

Researchers note that the unstable zone became obvious when compared with post-disaster imagery. In other words, the signal existed before the event, but it was recognised only through post-facto analysis.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, in a statement to NDTV, said, "The data from NISAR, including what its instruments have collected in the area of the flooding, has been and continues to be freely accessible to the public via the Alaska Satellite Facility Distributed Active Archive Center and ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal. Users can analyze the data to generally assess the risk of future disasters."

While ISRO has at least done a post-facto analysis, strangely NASA has not done any analysis of its own on the devastating Nepal floods.

That finding highlights perhaps the most important lesson emerging from the disaster. Satellites like NISAR can map vulnerability, identify unstable slopes, and detect accelerating deformation. They can help determine where danger exists and where risk is increasing. What they cannot currently do is predict the exact moment a glacier or mountain slope will collapse.

The challenge is compounded by scale. The Himalayas stretch across thousands of kilometres and contain 25,000-plus glaciers, hanging valleys, unstable rock faces and permafrost zones. Monitoring every square kilometre continuously would require enormous computing power, advanced artificial intelligence tools and round-the-clock analysis systems capable of processing radar imagery almost in real time.

Scientists also found evidence that climate change may have contributed to the disaster. Using satellite data, they determined that the summer of 2026 was exceptionally warm. Air temperatures remained significantly above the long-term average from 2001 to 2025 and frequently approached or exceeded one standard deviation above normal conditions. Daily temperatures reached between 8 and 9 degrees Celsius, making 2026 one of the warmest years in the 26-year record for the region. Such sustained warmth would have increased glacier melt, generated more meltwater and destabilised slopes already under stress.

The researchers argue that the Nepal disaster is unlikely to be an isolated event. They warn that warming temperatures, melting glaciers and unstable mountain slopes are creating conditions for more such cascading hazards across the Himalayas. Previous disasters, including the Chamoli rock-ice avalanche in Uttarakhand in 2021, pointed in the same direction. The Nepal catastrophe now strengthens the evidence that these events may become increasingly common in a warming world.

For ISRO and disaster management agencies, the study offers a powerful roadmap for the future. The answer is not simply launching better satellites. NISAR has already demonstrated that it can see the warning signs. The next step is building systems capable of continuously monitoring the entire Himalayan region, automatically flagging unusual glacier movements, identifying accelerating creep, and integrating satellite observations with climate, geological, and seismic data.

The Rasuwa flood has shown that satellites can reveal vulnerability. They can identify mountains that are becoming unstable. But predicting exactly when a glacier will break apart and unleash a deadly flood remains beyond the current capability of these eyes in the skies; one needs ground monitoring stations for that.

The world's single most expensive Earth imaging satellite saw the mountain move. The challenge now is ensuring that scientists are watching and offering a precise warning when it does. Bitter lessons were learned since NISAR flagged unusual changes in Nepal's Himalayas. Why did the alarm not ring remains a billion-dollar burning question.

title: Nepali Congress falls short of one-third women’s quota in central committee - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepali Congress falls short of one-third women’s quota in central committee  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Women have secured 69 of the 231 elected positions on the Nepali Congress central committee, accounting for 29.87 percent of elected members. All won seats reserved for women or allocated under the party’s inclusion categories.

The party’s statute requires women to make up at least one-third of executive committees at every level. The 297-member central committee comprises 231 elected members and 66 nominees appointed by the party president. Three women were elected to office-bearing posts, while 66 won central committee seats.

With 69 women elected, party president Gagan Thapa must nominate at least 30 women to the 66 appointed seats to bring female representation to 99, or one-third of the committee.

Although the new committee includes representatives from a wider range of ethnic, social and professional groups, no woman won an unreserved seat.

The party reserved one seat each for women in the posts of vice-president, general secretary and joint general secretary. Pushpa Bhusal, Dila Sangroula (Pant) and Pratima Gautam were elected to those positions, respectively. Sangroula is the first woman to be elected general secretary in the party’s history.

The central committee elected at the Nepali Congress’s 15th general convention, held in Kathmandu from October 4 to 9, reflects broader representation across ethnic communities and professional groups. However, women remain below the one-third threshold among elected members, leaving the party president to meet the quota through his nominations.

For the central committee election, the party allocated a set number of seats for women across open and inclusion-based categories. Beyond the seats designated specifically for women, female members were elected through quotas for Khas Arya, Indigenous nationalities, Madhesi, Dalit, Tharu and Muslim communities. Women also secured places representing all seven provinces, Kathmandu Valley, under-35 youth, disadvantaged regions, overseas Nepali party committees, professional groups and workers.

The breakdown includes 15 women elected through the women’s open category, eight each from Indigenous nationalities and Khas Arya groups, and five each from Madhesi and Dalit communities. Tharu and Muslim groups elected two women each.

Two women were elected from professional groups and two through overseas Nepali party committees. Workers, the disadvantaged region category and Kathmandu Valley each accounted for one woman member. Seven women under 35 were elected through provincial youth representation, while another seven won seats in the province-based women’s open category.

Twelve women contested positions outside the reserved categories, but none was elected, underscoring the limits of women’s representation in seats not set aside for them.

Sangroula said women had secured a more substantial presence in the party leadership than in the past.

title: Former President Bhandari calls for trilateral cooperation in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers - The Rising Nepal
description: Former President Bhandari calls for trilateral cooperation in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Mahendra Subedi, Xiong'an (China), Oct 24: Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari has called for stronger cooperation among Himalayan countries including Nepal, China and India in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers, developing early warning systems and coordinating disaster response.

Addressing the 2026 Global Governance Forum in China’s Xiong’an city of Hebei Province earlier today, the former President said that global governance is also linked to climate justice and added that the unprecedented natural disasters Nepal experienced in August have underscored the gravity of the challenge. She noted that the Himalayas are a shared natural heritage connected to regional water cycles, biodiversity and ecological balance.

Likewise, she advocated strengthening the United Nations as an effective institution reflecting the diversity and aspirations of the contemporary world, adding that peace and development are mutually reinforcing. Ending poverty and hunger, promoting human well-being and redirecting resources from the arms race towards development are shared responsibilities, the former President added.

Delivering her speech in Nepali language, the former President expressed confidence that the Forum would foster meaningful deliberations towards making the global governance system more just, inclusive and effective, while creating new opportunities for cooperation for world peace, sustainable development and shared prosperity.

On Nepal-China relations, she noted that the bilateral ties have evolved since ancient times through cultural exchanges, Buddhist philosophy and close people-to-people links. She said the relationship is rooted in the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and rests on mutual respect, trust and cooperation, reaffirming Nepal's unequivocal commitment to the One-China Policy.

Likewise, Bhandari said the world is undergoing rapid scientific and technological transformation while facing serious challenges including economic inequality, poverty, geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change and food insecurity. She was of the view that protectionism and unilateral approaches have complicated international cooperation, adding that such shared challenges cannot be resolved by any single nation and require dialogue and collective commitment.

The former president said that the international order founded on the UN Charter, international law and multilateralism has contributed significantly to peace and development, but reforms are needed to make it more inclusive, representative, transparent and effective.

"Global governance should not be shaped solely by the priorities of a limited number of nations," she said. "Differences among nations should be resolved through dialogue and diplomatic means," she added.

She further said the success of global governance should be measured by the positive changes it brings to people's lives.

The Forum was inaugurated by Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi on Friday evening.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s message was also delivered to the 2026 Global Governance Forum. “The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing,” Xi stated.

The Global Governance Initiative (GGI) was forwarded to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world, read the Chinese President’s message.

On the occasion, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang said all countries should uphold the multilateral trading system with the WTO at its core, keep development at the center of the international agenda, and fully implement the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

He also called for improving governance rules in emerging fields, turning new frontiers such as the deep sea, the polar regions and outer space into areas for international cooperation, and evolving an AI governance structure based on general consensus soon.

Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, the forum is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World."

Nearly 400 representatives from strategic, political, academic, business, media, and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN, attended the opening ceremony.(RSS)

title: A $1.3 Billion Satellite, The Deadly Nepal Flood And A Warning That Came Too Late - NDTV Profit

The NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite recorded the mountain moving weeks before the August 26 flood that killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal, but no one read the signal in time, according to a study by scientists at ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad.

The paper, by 12 researchers and published in the Journal of Indian Society of Remote Sensing, is the first scientific account of the disaster in Rasuwa district, NDTV reported.

What The Satellite Saw

NISAR's L-band radar data from June 20 to August 19 showed an unstable, fast-moving zone exactly where the slope later failed, the study said.

Between July 26 and August 19, the displacement grew larger and more coherent, with some pixels shifting more than five metres horizontally.

The researchers said the warning became obvious only when compared with post-disaster imagery. NISAR, which cost $1.3 billion and launched on July 30, 2025, sends data down about every 12 days.

How The Disaster Unfolded

Around 99 million cubic metres of glacier ice and permafrost rock broke off a hanging glacier north of Langtang Lirung peak, at about 5,130 metres, on the morning of August 26. The study compared the volume to about 115 Empire State Buildings.

The debris fell roughly 2,170 metres in total and travelled about 5.9 km along the valley floor before turning into a flood. It hit a 72-km stretch of the Lhende Khola and Trishuli river systems, destroying roads, bridges, buildings and tunnels, including along the Nepal-China trade corridor.

A second landslide about three hours later created a debris-dammed lake.

Nepal's disaster authority put the toll at 1,451 dead and 5,745 missing as of September 21, according to figures cited in the study. The seismic signal recorded at 8:22 a.m.IST was the avalanche's impact, not its trigger, the paper said.

Climate Link And Limits

The researchers said satellite data showed an exceptionally warm summer in 2026, which would have increased melt and weakened already stressed slopes.

They warned that such cascading hazards may become more common, pointing to the 2021 Chamoli disaster in Uttarakhand.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory told NDTV that NISAR data is freely available through the Alaska Satellite Facility and ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal.

The study said satellites can show which slopes are unstable but cannot predict when one will collapse. That, it said, needs ground monitoring stations, along with automated, near-real-time analysis of the Himalayas' more than 25,000 glaciers.

KATHMANDU: Nepali Communist Party (NCP) coordinator and former Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal Prachanda has said that a new political situation will emerge in the country in the near future.

Inaugurating the party’s awareness campaign at its central office in Parisdanda on Saturday, Dahal recalled the People’s War and expressed confidence that the party could regain public support despite challenges if it sincerely raised the issues affecting ordinary people.

Reflecting on the difficult early days of the movement, he said a campaign that began with a limited number of cadres gradually gained the support of millions, ultimately paving the way for historic political change in the country.

title: Not the best climate for climate finance - Nepali Times
description: Not the best climate for climate finance  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Nepal’s negotiators hailed the $21.6 million grant from the UN’s Loss & Damage Fund for the Trisuli Valley disaster on 26 August, but it was approved reluctantly, represents only 0.4% of the cost of recovery and reconstruction, and there are strings attached.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) this week provisionally approved the grant to Nepal for relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction two months after the flood catastrophe. It was announced in the run-up to a global climate summit (COP31) in Türkiye that starts 9 November.

Although Nepal is the first beneficiary of this scheme set up by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) during a previous climate summit in Egypt’s Sharm El-Sheikh in 2022, it came after three full decades of lobbying by developing countries for climate justice.

Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Waglé and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary wrote to the fund five days after the flood in August, seeking urgent assistance for a disaster they said was triggered by climate breakdown. Prime Minister Balendra Shah then made an impassioned speech at the UN General Assembly last month, calling for climate justice and solidarity.

Nepali officials have hailed the $20 million grant as a result of effective diplomacy and intense lobbying with the international community. However, some members of the FRLD Board at its extraordinary meeting on 22 October reportedly expressed reservations about the grant to Nepal, saying it should not set a precedent for pending claims by other countries to the Fund.

MILESTONE OR MILLSTONE?

“This landmark decision reflects the spirit of multilateral cooperation, climate justice and collective responsibility towards countries vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change,” said Maheshwar Dhakal of Nepal’s Ministry of Forests and Environment, who is currently serving with the FRLD from the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group.

“It is not only a significant milestone for Nepal but also a powerful message of hope and solidarity for developing countries,” he added.

Although Nepal has tried to put a brave face on the grant, $1.6 million of the $21.6 million will go for administrative costs, and the FRLD will have to approve a detailed proposal for where Nepal wants to spend the money. Rehabilitation and reconstruction will cost $4.7 billion, so the grant is only 0.4% of what is needed to rebuild.

Nepal’s Manjeet Dhakal is lead adviser to the LDC Chair on climate change, and says we should not expect the international community to accept all of Nepal’s demands, but added: “The fund was established for a purpose like this. And for the first time it has made a decision for our country, it’s symbolic and has long-term relevance in terms of setting a precedent.”

Only 1,500 remains of victims of the flood have been recovered, but at least 5,000 people are still unaccounted for. More than 60,000 people were directly affected by the flood, 15,000 of them children. Twelve operating and under construction hydropower plants generating 1,000MW were damaged or destroyed.

Climate skeptics have argued that the cascading disaster on 26 August was a result of geo-tectonic factors, and the heavy death toll and damage was because of recent settlements and infrastructure building along a vulnerable river valley, and cannot be entirely blamed on global warming.

In an interview with Nepali Times, Manjeet Dhakal disputed this: “We have enough resources and information such as World Weather Attribution strongly linking the floods to climate change and global warming.”

He says the Nepal government now needs to use its own rapid assessment of the damage, package them and submit a plan on utilising the fund for effective rehabilitation and reconstruction.

The Loss & Damage Fund operates through mechanisms like the Green Climate Fund (GCF) which in Nepal it works with accredited agencies like the Alternate Energy Promotion Centres (AEPC), the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) and NIMB bank for disbursement.

But experts say that ultimately it should be the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) that should lead the process because there may be bigger and more frequent Himalayan floods in future as the atmosphere warms.

“The $20 million was a limited fund for the short term, but our future preparedness needs serious consideration because there will be more and bigger disasters,” warns watershed scientist Madhukar Upadhyay. “Our strategy shouldn’t be to ask for money every time there is a disaster, it will never be sufficient and the funds are shrinking. We need to strengthen the capacity of local communities to deal with future disasters.”

The Nepal disaster will be front and centre of discussions at COP31 in Türkiye, and it will be an opportunity for its delegation to push the agenda of the vulnerability of mountain countries.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) released its Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return timed for the summit, warning that average global temperature would rise to 2.6°C above pre-industrial levels during this century. It said greenhouse emissions needed to be reduced by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2025 and 69% by 2040 to limit warming to 1.5°C.

“We are unlikely to hold the 1.5°C limit because the proposal to reduce fossil fuel dependence has been unpopular at recent COPs,” says Upadhaya, alluding to the United States and other countries backtracking on emission targets.

A 2.6°C rise would be catastrophic for the Himalaya which scientists say will then lose two-thirds of its remaining ice-cap, as glaciers shrink and the snowline moves up the mountain. If that happens, the Trisuli Valley flood will have been just a rehearsal for even bigger disasters to come.

High Asia is called the ‘Third Pole’ because it has the third largest volume of fresh water stored as ice, after the Arctic and Antarctica. If these ice caps melt, models show increased flow on Himalayan rivers until 2060 and steadily declining water volume thereafter for the 2 billion people who live downstream in Asia.

Says Manjeet Dhakal: “Despite economic downturns and geopolitics, the grant for Nepal shows that the international community is still committed to climate action. But it will not be enough to meet the consequences of a 2.6°C rise in global temperatures this century.”

title: Adaptation Fund approves three climate adaptation projects for Nepal - Khabarhub
description: Adaptation Fund approves three climate adaptation projects for Nepal  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Adaptation Fund has approved three climate adaptation project proposals for Nepal aimed at strengthening vulnerable communities, protecting ecosystems through nature-based solutions and improving early warning systems for floods and landslides.

The proposals were approved at the Fund’s 47th Board Meeting, which was also attended by Nepal’s representative on the Adaptation Fund Board, Naresh Sharma.

Sharma said the projects would help communities exposed to climate change build resilience, conserve ecosystems and improve preparedness for climate-related disasters through stronger early warning systems.

One of the approved proposals is the Green Koshi project, to be implemented by the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC). According to Sharma, the Board approved the project’s concept note with a proposed budget of USD 9.92 million. The initiative aims to strengthen climate resilience and conserve ecosystems through nature-based solutions.

Similarly, the Board approved a pre-concept note for the SAFE NIB project, which will be implemented by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). With a proposed budget of USD 300 million, the initiative aims to strengthen climate adaptation measures and improve flood and landslide early warning systems across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

The Board also approved a concept note for a project to build resilient communities through locally led, nature-based climate action in Lumbini Province. The project, to be implemented by the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat), has a proposed budget of approximately USD 4.99 million, Sharma said.

Meanwhile, the Fund’s next Board Meeting is expected to discuss a proposal to mobilise international climate adaptation finance for post-disaster management, recovery and reconstruction in the Bhote Koshi river area.

Sharma said the Board could not reach a decision on the initiative due to time constraints, but agreed to retain the agenda for further discussion at its next meeting in April.

The proposed initiative is expected to help expand access to international climate finance for communities affected by the August 26 floods in the Bhote Koshi river region, supporting their recovery and reconstruction efforts.

Established in 2001 under the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Adaptation Fund is an international climate finance mechanism that provides grants to vulnerable developing countries to strengthen their capacity to adapt to climate change and build resilience to its impacts. The Fund also serves the Paris Agreement.

title: Legal ground needed after Nepal opens letters of intent for private sector in cross-border power trade - The Kathmandu Post
description: Legal ground needed after Nepal opens letters of intent for private sector in cross-border power trade  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The government has decided to issue letters of intent but private firms seeking to trade electricity across Nepal’s borders will have to wait until the Electricity Act is amended and licences are granted to them.

The letter of intent, opened by a ministerial-level decision of the Ministry for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, is a preliminary approval intended to help the private sector study the market and identify potential partners.

Posting on social media, Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said that Nepal’s energy sector has entered in a new phase in which private companies would participate not only in electricity generation but also in cross-border trading.

The Nepal Electricity Authority is currently the only officially designated nodal agency for cross-border power trade between Nepal and India. Nepal also exports hydropower to Bangladesh using the transmission infrastructure of India.

The government designated the NEA as the nodal agency on February 28, 2020, to formulate plans for cross-border electricity imports and exports, as well as transmission lines and electricity trading, in coordination with India’s designated authority.

Private companies cannot buy or sell electricity until they obtain formal licences under the amended Electricity Act, 1992, officials said.

“The private sector will be able to obtain licences for electricity trading only after the law is amended. Only then can it engage in actual electricity trading,” said Sunil Paudel, joint-secretary and head of the Energy Division at the ministry. “The letter of intent merely opens the way for the private sector to prepare.”

The letter of intent helps the sector demonstrate its readiness and identify the basis for entering the electricity trading business.

The energy ministry has initiated the process of amending the Electricity Act, through a bill to establish the legal framework for licensing the private sector to trade electricity. The proposed amendment has been sent to the Ministry of Law for consent, according to the energy ministry. Once the ministry’s approval is received, the bill will have to be endorsed by a Cabinet meeting before it can be implemented.

Last Friday, Energy Minister Shrestha decided to issue letters of intent to the private sector in entering the electricity trading business. Twelve companies, including the Nepal Power Exchange, NIFRA Trading and Energy Exchange, Green Energy Power Trading and Trans Asia Power Trading, have applied.

The letters of intent will allow companies to identify potential markets and partners, assess investment opportunities and make the necessary preparations for electricity trading.

However, companies will not be allowed to implement power purchase agreements, book transmission capacity or use open access to transmit electricity on the basis of the letters alone.

The ministry has clarified that the letter of intent does not automatically entitle companies to licences and that the government will not be liable for any agreements entered into by the companies.

The letters of intent will remain valid for a maximum of two years. During this period, companies must submit progress reports to the energy ministry every three months.

Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), said the letters of intent were only the first step towards preparing for electricity trading and that considerable legal and technical clarity is still needed for the transaction.

Although companies can start discussions with Indian partners, establish offices, increase paid-up capital and hold annual general meetings, securing India’s approval and obtaining grid access remain crucial to cross-border electricity trading, he said.

Even after obtaining a licence in Nepal, the private sector will not be able to export electricity to India or other countries through the power exchange unless they receive approval under the cross-border electricity trade guidelines issued by India’s Central Electricity Authority.

Meanwhile, the Electricity Regulatory Commission has fixed a transmission wheeling charge of 57 paisa (NRs) per unit in October for the use of transmission lines. Energy promoters, however, have sought a revision, arguing that the rate is too high.

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal recorded 20 disaster-related incidents across the country in the past 24 hours, leaving eight people injured and causing property damage estimated at approximately Rs 2.41 million.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the incidents included fires, snakebites, altitude sickness, landslides, and wild animal attacks. The incidents occurred in various districts between 10:00 am on October 23 and 10:00 am on October 24.

NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Mahat said snakebite cases were reported in Saptari, Dhading, Gorkha, Kanchanpur, and Dadeldhura. Meanwhile, fire incidents were recorded in Morang, Sunsari, Bara, Nawalparasi East, Dang, Salyan, Kailali, and Dadeldhura.

Similarly, altitude sickness cases were reported in Manang and Dolpa, while a landslide occurred in Myagdi. Wild animal attacks were also reported in Kaski and Kailali.

The incidents left eight people injured, but no deaths were reported. The injured are receiving treatment at various health facilities, including hospitals outside their home districts.

The NDRRMA has urged the public to coordinate with local administrations, security agencies, and concerned authorities whenever potential disaster risks are identified. It has also advised people to follow official updates and instructions.

The authority emphasized that adopting preventive measures, remaining vigilant, and following safety guidelines during disasters can help minimize loss of life and property damage.
